result.text:
# Talk about making love before you do it
From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.
Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.
So what do the two of you think you’re about to do? One person may mean recreation or stress relief. The other may mean bonding or sacred practice. Maybe it is all of those, or something else neither of you has named.
It matters before sex because an honest answer could change the decision. Most couples wait until they’re already doing it, when the truth might interrupt what has begun. The earlier conversation can go places the later one often can’t. Having it is already part of the difference between making love together and merely having sex.
Meaning is only the beginning. What do you actually desire? What helps your body feel safe? Are there kinks or particular dynamics that matter to you? What has your history taught you about your erotic wiring? What reliably doesn’t work? How often do you each imagine wanting sex?
You may not know. A lot of people don’t yet, and that is still an answer. *I don’t know, but I’m willing to find out honestly with you* is a much better beginning than silently assuming the bodies will somehow negotiate everything on their own.
That candor is something you can assess now. Sexual compatibility isn’t just whether two bodies fit. It’s whether two people can stay honest while maximally exposed. If you can talk frankly before your clothes come off, you’ve already practiced some of the trust, attention, and willingness to be seen that making love requires.
Desire can diverge later. In long relationships, one person usually wants more sex, less sex, or different sex for at least some stretch. What would that mean, and how might you handle it? It’s one of the great factories of quiet resentment. Talking before either person is hurt won’t solve it in advance, but it gives you somewhere to begin.
